gaps: Sharpening each item's lie case produced the same shape every time: the tell lies where the carrier is cheap or dear for that investor for reasons unrelated to this deal (a two-partner fund, a fund late in its period, a house template). So the live question moved from which tells exist to what the founder must know about the fund's cost of each carrier before any behavior becomes a reading, and the second breath went looking for tells that survive without a denominator, tells whose reading belongs to another node, and tells that need the founder to act.
accepted: Ledger's clock: whether a yes is even available is read from the fund's own deployment record before the partner's appetite matters, since a fund in year four of a five-year investment period with half its capital uncalled must deploy and a fund that made nine investments in its first year and one in its third is holding reserves for its own portfolio, and both are visible in announced checks and filing dates before the first email; the carrier is the fund's ledger and not the partner, and it lies when the visible fund is not the vehicle that would write this check, an unannounced successor fund or an opportunity vehicle running on a different clock.

Partner's name on the door: whether the person across the table can carry a deal is read from whose name sits on the fund's last deals, its board seats and its announcements, not from the title on the website, since a venture partner, a principal, or an operating partner can refer but cannot spend; it lies in exactly one case, the newly made partner whose name is on nothing because their first deal is still to come, and who therefore has the strongest motive in the building to close one.

Neighbor in the portfolio: if the fund already holds a company in the founder's market, the meeting's purpose is set before it starts, and the tell is whether the partner names the neighbor unprompted, since an undisclosed neighbor makes the meeting intelligence gathered for it; it adds to cooperative-masks' alliance proposed to inventory your capabilities the check that can be run from the portfolio page before the alliance is proposed, and it lies at a fund that runs an index strategy and will honestly own two rivals, which its ledger shows as other such pairs.

Second body: partner attention is the fund's scarcest unit, so a second partner at the second meeting means the first has spent standing inside the partnership to bring one, as a medieval charter's witness list tells a historian which magnates the king needed present, while an associate-only follow-up, however warm, is still screening; a partner who writes the follow-up in their own words at midnight but cannot bring a second body is appetite without a vote, and the tell lies at a fund of two partners, where every meeting is a partner meeting and the reading must fall back to whether the meeting was moved to the founder's site.

Who sums up: the partnership's internal rank is read in the room from who interrupts whom and who restates the deal at the end, since the one who summarizes holds the pen the others will read from on Monday, the way a newcomer in a prison yard reads rank not from size but from who is deferred to; not who came, which is Second body, but the order of speech among those who did, and it lies at partnerships that perform equality, where the reading falls back to whom the others ask the last question.

Tense switch: an investor still deciding asks about the past, why the cohort churned, why this architecture, while an investor who has decided asks about the deal, round size, who else is in, whether there is room to lead, and the switch usually precedes any spoken yes by days; the sharpest form is the allocation question, how much can we take, which is addressed to the other investors through the founder, as an auction bidder who asks about the reserve has stopped inspecting the lot; it lies when a partner asks round size first to check the fund's check-size fit, which is a size question and not an allocation question.

Holdable sentence: an investor's words are read by whether they could later be quoted back against the speaker, so we would love to see more traction is a pass that keeps a free option on the company, while at this revenue with this retention, call me and we move in a week binds a metric, a threshold, and a date, as an employer who names a wage reopener date has conceded something and one who says we will look at it next year has not; the carrier is the cost of being quoted, and it lies when a fund rule such as a stage floor makes the vagueness honest rather than option-keeping, which is checked against the ledger.

Order of asks: a request for the data room before a partner-meeting date has been set reverses the usual order, in which a partner buys in, the partnership authorizes the work, and the room is opened, so it reads a partner who lacks standing and needs the data to win the room, or a fund whose associates screen on numbers before any partner looks; it is preparation rather than screening only when the ask arrives with a date attached, and it lies at growth funds where quantitative screening precedes every partner by design.

Shopping list: diligence questions divide by whether the answer is useful to someone other than the decider, so named customers with prices, a pipeline by account, and a roadmap by quarter are transferable to a portfolio company while the reason a cohort churned is not, and the test is whether the investor accepts anonymized accounts and founder-chosen reference names, since a decider needs the shape and a shopper needs the names; it lies at late-stage funds whose cohort work needs account-level data, separated by their willingness to route it through a third-party quality-of-earnings firm that returns only the shape.

Back-channel spent: a call to a reference the founder offered is process, but a call to someone the founder did not offer, a former employee, a former investor, a rival's founder, costs the caller a favor and is spent only near the decision, so learning of it, usually from the person called, reads that the partner meeting is close and names the objection being tested; the reverse of lead-time-floors' Seeking is telling, since here the investor's search is visible to the founder, and the sharper reading is the call not made, because a term sheet issued with no back-channel is a reservation and not a decision; it lies at large multi-stage funds whose research staff call everyone at screen, where the favor costs the partner nothing.

Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.

Exclusivity as confession: the length of the no-shop the investor asks for measures the work the investor has not yet done and the room to walk it wants to keep, so sixty days from a fund that has spent no back-channel is an option and ten days from one that has is a close; it adds to lead-time-floors' No-shop, which reads what the lock does to the founder's clock, by reading what the lock's length says about the investor's remaining doubt, and it lies where the length was set by counsel's template rather than by the partner.

Term as forecast: each protective term is a bet on a future state, so the redline shows the investor's private forecast, a participating preference pricing a middling exit as likely, a full ratchet pricing a down round, super pro-rata pricing a wish for more, information rights without a seat pricing a passive hold, as an arms treaty's inspection clauses name the breach each side expects; only deviations from the fund's standard paper read, since house paper forecasts nothing, and the founder learns the standard from other founders who took it; it lies where the partner has not read what counsel sent.

residue.item: Partner's own keyboard: a partner who writes the follow-up in their own words at odd hours has taken the deal into their own hands.
residue.why: Merged into Second body as its discriminator: the keyboard reads personal appetite and the second body reads institutional standing, and the instructive case is the partner who has the first and cannot get the second, which the merged item now states.

residue.item: Meeting moved to the founder's site: a partner who travels spends a day.
residue.why: Merged into Second body as the fallback carrier for the case where the second body is cheap (a two-partner fund); alone it is the same mechanism, senior hours spent, with a different unit.

residue.item: Founders the investor offers as references: whether the list includes founders whose companies failed.
residue.why: Rejected: it reads how the investor will behave after the wire, not where their decision on this deal sits; out of the item type and kept as the gate's boundary case.

residue.item: Wire before paper: an investor who wires or bridges before the documents close.
residue.why: Rejected: it is the terminal state of an interval rather than a carrier of its own, and without Ledger's clock it reads must-deploy as often as appetite; no independent reading.

gate: declared modality, recognizable distinction, defensible seriation and conditional relations
limits: Authored analytical fieldwork from composite cases in venture practice; no item is a documented history of any named fund, and the remote cases (charter witness lists, kidnappers' deadlines, treaty inspection clauses, wage reopeners) are simplified to expose one mechanism each.

The seriation is an itinerary of where the founder must stand to see the carrier, not a ranking of reliability or importance; a tell late on the route is not a better tell, and map edges are conditional authored claims.

Every tell is read against a denominator, the fund's size, age, decision rule, and the partner's tenure, which the map treats as readable from the ledger; where the ledger is private, an unannounced vehicle or a family office, the readings above are undefined, and the map does not claim the ledger is always public.

Tells about the investor's future conduct, how they behave in a down round or whom they let the founder call, are outside the item type except at Next-round hand, where past conduct becomes the next founder's ledger; the map reads position, not character.

The map reads the investor and does not say what the founder should do with the reading; tells the investor can fake cheaply once the map is known, a second body sent as theater, a fuse set for show, are named as lies inside items but are not mapped as a class.

gaps: The denominator question yielded a tell that transfers to another investor (Borrowed eyes), a tell in the wording of a no that says whether a vote happened (Named objection), a tell that exists only if the founder moves (Let it lapse), and the tell that arrives too late and becomes the next founder's ledger (Next-round hand), which turned the route from a line into a loop through other founders. Second-meeting clock and Redline tempo collapsed into one mechanism, Queue interval, at two stations. The territory pointer 'investor tells' stands; the of-sentence now carries the station axis and the founder's own move as a station.
accepted: Queue interval: an interval the founder is made to wait measures this deal's rank in a queue the founder cannot see, so the days before the second meeting read the partner's queue against whatever else that partner saw this week, and after signing the days before counsel returns a standard document read the fund's closing queue and whether it is waiting on something unsaid, a co-investor, a consent, a successor fund; it adds to lead-time-floors' Partner meeting, which reads what the calendar does to the founder's runway, by reading what the interval says about the investor's ordering, and it lies whenever the interval is the fund's clock rather than the partner's, in August, in December, or under must-deploy, which is why a fast second meeting from a fund late in its period reads the ledger and not the partner.

Borrowed eyes: an investor whose first question is who else is in holds a position that is a function of another investor's, so the founder is reading the wrong node and every later tell from this investor should be re-read as a tell about the lead it follows, a day late; it lies when the question is about round mechanics from a fund that never leads and honestly needs a lead to set terms, which its ledger shows as a record of follows.

Named objection: a no that states the specific objection that won reveals that a vote happened and the sponsor argued and lost, since only someone who fought the objection can name it exactly, while a no attributed to the partnership in generic terms reveals that the deal never reached the room; it adds to deal-deaths' Champion's single-tender want, which reads how a sponsor's leaving kills a deal, by reading from the wording of the no whether a sponsor existed at all, and it lies when a partner who killed the deal alone reads back the founder's own weakest slide as the objection.

Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; likewise offering anonymized accounts reads the shopper and declining the early data room reads whether a partner date appears; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.

Next-round hand: the investor's position is finally read after the wire, at the next round, in whether the fund takes its pro-rata, bridges a gap, or lets another lead mark the company down, which arrives too late for this raise and is the first tell for the next founder, because a fund's last three checks and its follow-ons are exactly the post-wire hands that other founders could not use in time, so the outside-readable ledger is made of other people's late tells; it lies when the fund's reserves ran out for reasons of vintage rather than belief, which Ledger's clock separates.

residue.item: Redline tempo: the speed at which the investor's counsel turns a standard document after signing.
residue.why: Merged into Queue interval: the same mechanism, an interval reading rank in a queue the founder cannot see, at a second station on the route; the merged item names both queues and the case (fast meeting, slow redline) that shows they are different queues.

residue.item: Question already answered: an investor who asks something they plainly know from a portfolio company is testing honesty, not learning.
residue.why: Held as unresolved seed: it is a test the investor runs on the founder rather than a tell the founder reads off the investor, and admitting it would flip the map's direction; it belongs to a sibling map of founder-tells if one is ever made.

residue.item: Fund's own raise: a fund raising its successor wants marks and announcements, and asks to announce the round or asks who else is in for its own deck.
residue.why: Held: the state is real and distinct, but the carriers it uses, filing dates and the who-else-is-in question, are already read by Ledger's clock and Borrowed eyes; it needs a carrier of its own (the press-release ask, perhaps) before admission.

neighbors.left: Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.

neighbors.separating_case: A sheet with a forty-eight-hour fuse and a sixty-day no-shop: the fuse says the investor fears a rival sheet this week, the no-shop says the investor has not decided, and together they read an investor trying to freeze the market before doing the work; a sheet with a ten-day fuse and a ten-day no-shop is the opposite object, an investor who has decided and fears nobody. The two clocks read two different states, the investor's estimate of the founder's alternatives and the investor's own remaining doubt, and can point in opposite directions on one page.

checks.boundary_case: Which founders the investor lets you call is a tempting nonmember: it is read from what the investor does rather than says, but it reads how the investor will behave after the wire, their conduct in a down round, not where their decision on this deal sits, so it is out of type. Next-round hand is in on exactly that contrast, since it reads the fund's position (reserves, belief) at the point where past conduct becomes another founder's ledger.
checks.form_inference: The map shows a loop the sequence conceals: Next-round hand → Ledger's clock, where the last tell of one raise, unusable in time, is the first tell of the next founder's, so the outside-readable half of the route is made of other founders' late tells. It shows a dependency, Ledger's clock → Queue interval and Partner's name on the door → Second body, where a behavior has no reading until its denominator has been read. It shows a fork, Back-channel spent → Fuse length, where the same expiry clause is a reservation or a decision depending on what preceded it. It shows a passage between nodes, Borrowed eyes → Tense switch, where the reading transfers to a different investor and this one's tells are discarded. And it shows a passage between levels, Let it lapse → Fuse length, from observation to experiment, where a tell has no settled reading until the founder acts.
checks.target_preserved: Self-read only. Each admitted item names a distinct carrier, a distinct state it reveals, and a distinct case where it lies; the strange members (a tell that reads the founder's own price off the investor's fear, a tell that transfers to another node, a tell that exists only if the founder moves, a tell that arrives too late and becomes someone else's first tell) are kept as mechanisms rather than softened into a list of red flags.

next_crossfield_opening: Tells that require the reader to act: connect Let it lapse with importance-detectors' stress-event residence and witness-architectures' Silence priced as guilt; ask which counterparty states can be read only by imposing a cost on the reader, and whether a probe-tell can ever be run twice on the same counterparty.

gaps: The declared type says the tell is read off what the investor spends, forgoes, sequences, or signs rather than says, yet five members (Tense switch, Borrowed eyes, Holdable sentence, Named objection, the unprompted naming in Neighbor in the portfolio) are read off speech, each rescued by a cost inside the speech: quotability, whether inspection follows a question, particularity of a no. The map's real item type is a cost the investor pays or forgoes without pricing the reading into it, whether it sits in a calendar, a signature, or a sentence. Under-stating it let Borrowed eyes collapse into Tense switch on the competitive-check case (repaired by moving the carrier to whether inspection follows the answer), ruled Wire before paper out on a denominator caveat every admitted item carries, and left the map reading every cost spent inside the fund and on the market while reading none spent toward the founder.
accepted: Partner's name on the door: whether the person across the table can carry a deal is read from whose name sits on the fund's last deals, its board seats and its announcements, not from the title on the website, since a venture partner, a principal, or an operating partner can refer but cannot spend; it lies most instructively at the newly made partner whose name is on nothing because their first deal is still to come, and who therefore has the strongest motive in the building to close one, and it also lies at the partner hired laterally, whose deals sit on another fund's ledger, and at funds that seat a different partner on the board than the one who sponsored the deal, where the seat list reads bandwidth and not standing.

Borrowed eyes: an investor who asks who else is in before any question about the company, and whose questions about the company arrive only after the answer names a lead, or never, holds a position that is a function of another investor's, so the founder is reading the wrong node and every later tell from this investor should be re-read as a tell about the lead it follows, a day late; not the same question asked first by an investor who then inspects, which checks whether the round is already spoken for, and it lies when the question is about round mechanics from a fund that never leads and honestly needs a lead to set terms, which its ledger shows as a record of follows.

Named objection: a no that states the objection that won, in terms particular to this company, reads as a vote that happened and a sponsor who argued and lost, since only someone who fought the objection can name it exactly, while a no attributed to the partnership in generic terms reads as a deal that never reached the room; not a specific no that is a fund rule, a stage floor or a sector the fund does not do, which is exact without any vote, and it adds to deal-deaths' Champion's single-tender want, which reads how a sponsor's leaving kills a deal, by reading from the wording of the no whether a sponsor existed at all; it lies when a partner who killed the deal alone reads back the founder's own weakest slide as the objection.

Back-channel spent: a call to a reference the founder offered is process, but a call to someone the founder did not offer, a former employee, a former investor, a rival's founder, costs the caller a favor and is spent only near the decision, so learning of it, usually from the person called, reads that the partner meeting is close and names the objection being tested; the reverse of lead-time-floors' Seeking is telling, since here the investor's search is visible to the founder, and the sharper reading is the call not made, because a term sheet issued with no back-channel is a reservation and not a decision wherever there was someone to call; it lies at large multi-stage funds whose research staff call everyone at screen, where the favor costs the partner nothing, and it is undefined at pre-seed, where no former employee, investor, or rival exists to be called and the absent call reads nothing.

Term as forecast: each protective term is a bet on a future state, so the redline shows the investor's private forecast, a participating preference pricing a middling exit as likely, a full ratchet pricing a down round, super pro-rata pricing a wish for more, information rights without a seat pricing a passive hold, as an arms treaty's inspection clauses name the breach each side expects; only deviations from the fund's standard paper read, since house paper forecasts nothing, and the founder learns the standard from other founders who took it; it lies where the partner has not read what counsel sent, and where a term was carried forward from the company's own prior paper, which forecasts the last investor's fear and not this one's.

Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; the same move exists at Shopping list and Order of asks, whose tests become probes when the founder makes the offer or the refusal first; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.

residue.item: Critic's observation that the of-sentence's 'rather than says' undersells the map's own members, which are read off the unpriced cost inside a calendar, a signature, or a sentence
residue.why: Offered as the map's sharper item type, not as a repair to the of-sentence; the of-sentence is left as authored and the sharper type is named in target_preserved and in the critic's review line, so a later breath can retitle if the founder-directed costs in the seed are admitted.

residue.item: Wire before paper (breath-one residue): an investor who wires or bridges before the documents close
residue.why: The critic holds that its rejection on the denominator caveat was not a reason, since every admitted item carries that caveat, and that it is the largest unpriced cost on the route; not readmitted here because the repairer adds no items beyond the critic's repairs, and it is carried in the seed as the first member of the founder-directed class.

limits: Authored analytical fieldwork from composite cases in venture practice; no item is a documented history of any named fund, and the remote cases (charter witness lists, kidnappers' deadlines, treaty inspection clauses, wage reopeners, the prison yard's order of deference, the auction bidder's reserve question) are simplified to expose one mechanism each.

Every tell is read against a denominator, the fund's size, age, decision rule, and the partner's tenure, which the map treats as readable from the ledger; the public ledger is partial even where it exists, since uncalled capital is not public for most funds and announced checks undercount deployment, so Ledger's clock is an estimate from a sample and not a record; where the ledger is private, an unannounced vehicle or a family office, the readings above are undefined, and the map does not claim the ledger is always public.
seed: Costs the investor spends toward the founder before the wire: a portfolio founder who calls unprompted to vouch for the partner, a customer introduction made before any sheet, a bridge wired before paper. These are the pre-wire mirror of Next-round hand, the fund spending its own favors or capital to hold a deal it has not yet won, and the map currently reads every cost spent inside the fund and on the market and none spent toward the founder. The residue item Wire before paper belongs here and was rejected on the denominator caveat every admitted item carries, which is not a reason. A cheaper instrument for the same class: deck telemetry, where a second partner's open on the data room is Second body before the meeting happens.
